nodes.statement: The expected saving of size (log log log N)^-delta is a consequence of three factors: first, the Siegel--Walfisz theorem restricts the range of moduli to a power of log N; second, the W-trick loses another log iteration; third, the final log iteration is lost due to the sparseness of high-rank Bohr sets. It should also be mentioned that this paper improves on a previous preprint of the authors, in which the weaker result E(N,2,3)ll N^1-delta was shown. The approach we take here is technically simpler in addition to producing a stronger result. In particular, the current approach does not require the spectral theory of automorphic forms, which featured in due to the use of Kloosterman sum estimates of Deshouillers--Iwaniec and their variants. Apart from a similar treatment of sieves for large prime factors, the approach here is independent of and supersedes it.
nodes.raw_latex:
The expected saving of size $(\log \log \log N)^{-\delta}$ is a consequence of three factors: first, the Siegel--Walfisz theorem restricts the range of moduli to a power of $\log N$; second, the $W$-trick loses another $\log$ iteration; third, the final $\log$ iteration is lost due to the sparseness of high-rank Bohr sets. 

It should also be mentioned that this paper improves on a previous preprint of the authors~\cite{grimmelt-teravainen}, in which the weaker result $E(N,2,3)\ll N^{1-\delta}$ was shown. The approach we take here is technically simpler in addition to producing a stronger result. In particular, the current approach does not require the spectral theory of automorphic forms, which featured in~\cite{grimmelt-teravainen} due to the use of Kloosterman sum estimates of Deshouillers--Iwaniec~\cite{DI} and their variants. Apart from a similar treatment of sieves for large prime factors, the approach here is independent of~\cite{grimmelt-teravainen} and supersedes it.

nodes.name: a normalised indicator for the Chen primes
nodes.statement: We define a normalised indicator for the Chen primes as Lambda_Chen(n)coloneqq Lambda(n)Lambda_2(n+2). Theorem~ follows if we can show a reasonable lower bound for sum_n_1+n_2=mLambda_Chen(n_1)Lambda_Chen(n_2) for all but O(N^1-delta) natural numbers mleq N, mequiv 4 pmod6.
nodes.raw_latex:
We define a normalised indicator for the Chen primes as 
$$\Lambda_{\text{Chen}}(n)\coloneqq \Lambda(n)\Lambda_2(n+2).$$
Theorem~\ref{MT1} follows if we can show a reasonable lower bound for
\begin{align}\label{eq:maintarget}
    	\sum_{n_1+n_2=m}\Lambda_{\text{Chen}}(n_1)\Lambda_{\text{Chen}}(n_2)
\end{align}
for all but $O(N^{1-\delta})$ natural numbers $m\leq N, m\equiv 4 \pmod{6}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
The step~\eqref{eq:outlinepresievasymp} is a consequence of a fundamental lemma-type result that allows us to handle $P$-rough numbers in essentially any additive setup easily with high precision, as long as $(\log m)/(\log P)$ is large enough in absolute terms. 

We now outline what goes into each of the steps in the chain of inequalities and approximations~\eqref{eq_outline1}--\eqref{eq_outline4}. The sieve $\omega_{\text{Chen}}$ in~\eqref{eq_outline1} is a combination of the usual sieve-switching approach for Chen primes with a separate sieve for small prime factors. In reality, one needs to be slightly more careful, as the product of two lower bound sieves is not a lower bound sieve. Note that for our purposes $\Lambda_{E_3}$ behaves the same way as $\Lambda$. In step~\eqref{eq_outline2}, we remove the contribution of the main-sieves by~\eqref{eq:intromainsieveremoval}. In step~\eqref{eq_outline3}, we replace the primes (respectively, the $E_3$-numbers) with the much easier-to-handle $P$-Cram\'er model; this follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:F-P-C_intro} or more precisely from~\eqref{eq:LambdatorP}. The final step~\eqref{eq_outline4} is a consequence of~\eqref{eq:introfundamental}.

nodes.statement: The result follows the construction in, with two differences: we skip the pre-sieving (which actually simplifies the proof), and we make statements about the sieve weights instead of the sifted set. We give the resulting details below. We only consider the case of a lower bound sieve, the upper bound being very similar. By the standard construction of the linear sieve (see) we have for any D_0 1_pmid n implies pnot in [P,z)geq sum_substackdmid n\\ din D^-(D_0)mu(d)1_pmid d implies p in [P,z), where D^-(D_0) is given by as D^-(D_0)=\d=p_1cdots p_r : p_1>ldots > p_r, p_1cdots p_m p_m^2 <D_0 for all m even\. As shown in, as long as z<sqrtD_0, this set already enjoys good factorisation properties. To make use of those, we call r the number of prime divisors of d and split the relevant primes into short intervals. Let eta=varepsilon^9, set D_0=D^1/(1+eta), and let D_1, ldots, D_r run over numbers of the type P^(1+eta)^j. Define for even r D_r=\(D_1,ldots,D_r)colon D_rleq ldots leq D_1 leq sqrtD_0, D_1ldots D_m D_m^2<D_0, mleq r, m even\ and for odd r D_r=\(D_1,ldots,D_r)colon D_rleq ldots leq D_1 leq D_0, D_1ldots D_m D_m^2<D_0, m< r, m even\. Note that the condition mequiv r pmod 2 in is a typo. For the second statement, we use the well known estimate for Gauss sums that gives for primitive characters max_b(r)bigl|sum_a(r)chi(a) e_r(ab)bigr|leq r^1/2.         &\psi(n)(g*b_R)(n)-(\psi g)*b_R(n)\\
        =&\sum_{|m|\leq N/R^4}(\psi(n)-\psi(n-m))g(n-m)b_R(m)\\
        \ll&  \sup_{|t-n|\leq N/R^4} |\psi'(t)| \sum_{|m|\leq N/R^4}  |m g(n-m) b_R(m)| \\

Using the formula c_q(n)=sum_dmid (q,n)dmuleft(fracqdright) for Ramanujan sums (which is easily verified by noting that both sides are multiplicative in q), we can write Lambda_R,r(n)&=sum_dmid ndmu(d)sum_substackqequiv 0pmod d\\ (q,r)=1fracmu(q)^2varphi(q)Gleft(fraclog(qr)log Rright)nonumber\\ &=sum_substackdmid n\\ (d,r)=1fracdmu(d)varphi(d)sum_substackell \\ (ell,dr)=1fracmu(ell)^2varphi(ell)Gleft(fraclog (ell dr)log Rright), where, writing the square-free q with dmid q as q=dell with (d,ell)=1, we used mu(q)mu(q/d)=mu(d)mu(q)^2 to extract dmu(d) and the multiplicativity varphi(dell)=varphi(d)varphi(ell), mu(dell)^2=mu(ell)^2. To proceed further, we follow a Fourier-analytic approach similar to. Let psi be the Fourier transform of tmapsto e^t G(t). Then by Fourier inversion for xin R we have e^xG(x) =int_Rpsi(xi)e^-ixi x\,d xi. By the smoothness of G, for any B>0 we have psi(t)ll_B (1+|t|)^-B. Plugging~ into~, we get Lambda_R,r(n)= int_mathbb Rpsi(xi) r^-(1-ixi)/log R sum_substackdmid n\\ (d,r)=1fracdmu(d)varphi(d)d^(1-ixi)/log R sum_substackell \\ (ell,dr)=1fracmu(ell)^2varphi(ell)ell^(1-ixi)/log R \,d xi. Here the last equality uses the identity bigl(1+tfrac1(p_2-1)p_2^sbigr)bigl(1-tfracp_2(p_2-1)p_2^sbigl(1+tfrac1(p_2-1)p_2^sbigr)^-1bigr)=1-p_2^-s with s=(1-ixi)/log R, the factor 1+tfrac1(p_2-1)p_2^s for each p_2mid n being drawn from the product over p_1. To estimate the product over p_1, we first note that since rleq R^2 we have fracrvarphi(r) prod_pmid r Bigl(1+frac1(p-1)p^(1-ixi)/log R Bigr)^-1&ll prod_pmid r Bigl(1+frac1p-1Bigr)Bigl(1+frac1(p-1)p^1/log RBigr)^-1\\ &ll prod_pmid r Bigl(1+frac1-p^-1/log Rp-1Bigr)\\&ll prod_pmid r Bigl(1+Obigl(fraclog pp log Rbigr)Bigr)\\ &ll exp Bigl(Obigl(sum_pleq log r fraclog pp log Rbigr) Bigr)\\ &ll 1. Writing log n=log b+log(n/b), we can estimate T_1 with the type I bound. For T_2, we split b,c into dyadic intervals (N_1/2,N_1],(N_2/2,N_2] and observe that the sum is empty unless N/2<N_1 N_2<4N'. Taking the maximum over theta and incorporating nu_theta,c and e(-theta b) into the coefficients gives a valid type II sum after observing that either N_1leq 2sqrtN' or N_2leq 2sqrtN'. nodes.statement: The beta sieve is a combinatorial sieve that is constructed by iteration with certain cutoff parameters, see. From this it follows immediately that for the upper bound sieve Omega we have the identity Omega(n)=r_P_1(n)+ prod_p < P_1left(1-frac1pright)^-1sum_r oddV_r(n), and similarly for the lower bound sieve omega we have omega(n)=r_P_1(n)- prod_p < P_1left(1-frac1pright)^-1sum_r evenV_r(n), where V_r(n)=sum_substackp_1cdots p_r mid n\\ p_imid P(P_1), \,\,\, p_r<p_r-1<ldots <p_1 \\ p_1p_2cdots p_r p_r^betageq D_1 \\ p_1p_2cdots p_hp_h^beta <D_1 for all h<r, hequiv rpmod 2 1_(n/(p_1cdots p_r),P(p_r))=1. By, in the last sum we have p_rgeq P_1^bigl(fracbeta-1beta+1bigr)^r/2. We also have D_1leq p_1^r+betaleq P_1^r+beta, which is impossible unless rgeq s-beta. We complete the proof by repeating the argument in: In the sum defining V_r, the distinct primes p_imidP(P_1) satisfy p_ige5, so writing nu(n) for the number of prime divisors of n we have nu(n)geq r so that 2^nu(n)-rgeq 1. Hence, V_r(n)leq 1_(n,P_r/2)=1 2^nu(n)-r sum_k mid n 1 leq 1_(n,P_r/2)=1 tau(n)^2 2^-r. Writing r=2r'+1 or r=2r', respectively for the case of an upper bound or lower bound sieve, the lemma follows.

Furthermore, the arising condition that b,m-bequiv 5 pmod(6,r) is automatic by the support of a. From this point, we can follow the argument in the proof of Proposition~ verbatim, apart from the additional condition that (d_1d_2d_3d_4,r)=1 and the additional factor 1/r when approximating the sum over n. Explicitly, for (6,r)=1 the innermost sum equals tfracX6r[d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4]+O(1), the term O(1) contributing O(rD_1^4(log P_1)^4) after summation over the d_i and over bpmod r. Naturally all the S_i are functions of both m and r. By the nature of the singular series being a product of local solution densities (or a short direct verification), we see that fracS_1(m,r)rprod_pmid rBigl(1-tfrac1pBigr)^-4=fracS(m)S'(m,r). We set sigma_1(m)coloneqqfracS_3(m,r)S_1(m,r). An application of the triangle inequality immediately shows |sigma_1|leq 1. The sum S_2 is multiplicative in r. Indeed, for coprime r=r_1r_2 the Chinese Remainder Theorem and chi=chi_r_1chi_r_2 factor the sum as S_2(m,r_1)S_2(m,r_2). Using a simple inclusion-exclusion argument and orthogonality of characters gives |S_2(m,r)|ll r^o(1). This shows~. For the case a=a_2 we observe 1_chi(b)=chi(b+2)=1=1_(b(b+2),r)=1(1+chi(b))(1+chi(b+2))/4 so that 8sum_b(r)a_2(b)=S_1-S_3-S_4+S_5-S_6+O_epsilonbigl(r^1/2+epsilonbigr), where S_1 and S_3 are as above and S_4&= sum_b(r)chi(b+2)chi(m-b)1_(b(m-b+2),r)=1,\\ S_5&=sum_b(r)chi(b+2)1_(b(m-b)(m-b+2),r)=1,\\ S_6&=sum_b(r)chi(b)chi(b+2)chi(m-b)1_(m-b+2,r)=1. Here the error term O_epsilon(r^1/2+epsilon) collects the three single- and double-character sums sum_b(r)chi(b), sum_b(r)chi(b)chi(b+2) and sum_b(r)chi(m-b) arising in the expansion, each ll_epsilon r^1/2+epsilon as for S_5,S_6. Finally, since chi is primitive and quadratic we have that r/(4,r) is square-free. Thus, using that S_6 is multiplicative in r, a simple inclusion-exclusion argument, and the Weil bound, we get |S_6(m,r)|ll_epsilon r^1/2+epsilon. This shows~ and completes the proof.

nodes.statement: It is not difficult to calculate sigma_1(m) and sigma_2(m) and write them as products of local densities. However, when compared to the related case of widetildeS(m) in, the treatment is more involved. In particular the primes 3, 5 and 7 need to be handled separately. To simply show the existence of suitable representations of m as in Theorem~, the precise evaluation of the functions sigma_i plays no role. It matters only that both |sigma_1| and |sigma_2| are 1-bounded and that sigma_1 appears with different signs in~ and~.
nodes.raw_latex: It is not difficult to calculate $\sigma_1(m)$ and $\sigma_2(m)$ and write them as products of local densities. However, when compared to the related case of $\widetilde{\mathfrak{S}}(m)$ in~\cite{mv}, the treatment is more involved. In particular the primes $3$, $5$ and $7$ need to be handled separately. To simply show the existence of suitable representations of $m$ as in Theorem~\ref{MT1}, the precise evaluation of the functions $\sigma_i$ plays no role. It matters only that both $|\sigma_1|$ and $|\sigma_2|$ are $1$-bounded and that $\sigma_1$ appears with different signs in~\eqref{eq_fundex_1} and~\eqref{eq_fundex_2}.

nodes.name: An upper bound for correlations of multiplicative functions
nodes.statement: Let Ageq 1 be fixed. Let h:Nto R_geq 0 be a multiplicative function that satisfies h(n)leq n^o(1) and h(p^k)leq A^k for all primes p and all kin N. Let log Nleq P'_1,P'_2,P'_3 leq N. Then, for any min [5N/4,7N/4] and m equiv 4pmod 6, we have &sum_N/2< nleq Nh(n)(tau^2r_P'_1)(n+2)(tau^2r_P'_2)(m-n)(tau^2r_P'_3)(m-n+2)\\ ll& fracNlog NS(m) prod_i=1^3 nonumber left(fraclog Nlog P'_iright)^3 prod_p<Nleft(1+frach(p)pright)prod_substackpmid m (m+2)(m+4)\\ pgeq min\P'_1,P'_2,P'_3\Bigl(1+fracO(1)pBigr). The same bound holds if h(n) swaps places with any of the other weights on n+2,m-n,m-n+2.

nodes.name: Correlations of absolute values of sieve weights
nodes.statement: Let mgeq 10 be an integer, and let varepsilon>1/log log m and N^varepsilon leq R, P_1leq N. For 1leq i leq 3, let the functions f_iin \ omega, Omega \ be pre-sieves as in Definition~, and let P_1^500leq D_1leq N^1/100. Let H_R be as in Theorem~. Then for any min [5N/4,7N/4] and m equiv 4pmod 6, we have sum_N/2<nleq NH_R(n) |f_ 1(n+2)||f_2(m-n)||f_3(m-n+2)|ll varepsilon^-10NS(m). The same bound holds if H_R(n) swaps places with any of the other weights on n+2,m-n,m-n+2.

nodes.statement: We start by relating all the summands to multiplicative functions. We recall that H_R(n)= (log R) tau(n)int_mathbb Rfrach_xi(n)(1+|xi|)^10 \,d xi, where h_xi(p)=minBigl\1,10(1+|xi|)fraclog plog R Bigr\. We next apply Lemma~ and recall the notation therein (in particular, P_r=P(P_1^bigl(fracbeta-1beta+1bigr)^r)). Since |f_i(n)|le r_P_1(n)+|f_i(n)-r_P_1(n)| and r_P_1(n)=prod_p<P_1bigl(1-frac1pbigr)^-11_(n,P_0)=1 is the r=0 term of the sum below, we get the upper bound |f_i(n)|ll prod_p<P_1left(1-frac1pright)^-1 tau(n)^2 sum_rgeq 04^-r1_(n,P_r)=1. Write a(r)coloneqq((beta-1)/(beta+1))^r with beta=200. Then by Mertens' theorem, prod_p< P_1left(1-frac1pright)^-1 1_(n,P_r)=1 = &prod_P_1^a(r)leq p < P_1 left(1-frac1pright)^-1 r_P_1^a(r)(n)\\ ll & a(r)^-1 r_P_1^a(r)(n). Thus, nonumber &sum_N/2<nleq NH_R(n) |f_ 1(n+2)||f_2(m-n)||f_3(m-n+2)|\\ ll &(log R) int_mathbb Rfrac1(1+|xi|)^10 sum_r_1,r_2,r_3 geq 0 4^-r_1-r_2-r_3a(r_1)^-1a(r_2)^-1a(r_3)^-1 H(xi,r_1,r_2,r_3) \,d xi, where H(xi,r_1,r_2,r_3)=sum_N/2<nleq N tau(n)h_xi(n) (tau^2 r_P_1^a(r_1))(n+2)(tau^2 r_P_1^a(r_2))(m-n)(tau^2 r_P_1^a(r_3))(m-n+2). This is amenable for an application of Lemma~ (with h(p)=2h_xi(p)). To prepare this application, we estimate left|prod_p<Nleft(1+frac2 h_xi(p)pright)right|leq& expleft(sum_pleq Nfrac2 h_xi(p)pright)\\ ll & expBigl(sum_pleq R^1/(1+|xi|)frac20(1+|xi|)log pplog R+sum_R^1/(1+|xi|)<pleq Nfrac2pBigr)\\ ll& Bigl(fraclog Nlog RBigr)^2(1+|xi|)^2, by a trivial bound for |xi|>10/log R and Mertens' theorem in the complementary range. Consequently, an application of Lemma~ gives &H(xi,r_1,r_2,r_3)\\ ll& Bigl(fraclog Nlog RBigr)^2(1+|xi|)^2fracNlog NS(m) prod_i=1^3 left(fraclog Nlog P_1^a(r_i)right)^3 prod_substackpmid m (m+2)(m+4)\\ pgeq min\P_1^a(r_1),P_1^a(r_2),P_1^a(r_3)\Bigl(1+fracO(1)pBigr). Plugging this into~, the integral over xi converges and we get the upper bound ll N S(m)fraclog Nlog R Bigl(fraclog Nlog P_1Bigr)^9 left(sum_rgeq 04^-ra(r)^-4prod_substackpmid m (m+2)(m+4)\\ pgeq P_1^a(r)Bigl(1+fracO(1)pBigr) right)^3. Since R,P_1geq N^varepsilon, we have fraclog Nlog R Bigl(fraclog Nlog P_1Bigr)^9leq varepsilon^-10, so that it only remains to show that the sum over r converges. If P_1^a(r)>log m, then prod_substackpmid m (m+2)(m+4)\\ pgeq P_1^a(r)Bigl(1+fracO(1)pBigr)ll 1. On the other hand, we always have prod_substackpmid m (m+2)(m+4)\\ pgeq P_1^a(r)Bigl(1+fracO(1)pBigr)ll log log m. Also, recalling beta=200, we have a(1)^-4/4= left(fracbeta+1beta-1right)^4/4<1/3. Thus, sum_rgeq 04^-ra(r)^-4prod_substackpmid m (m+2)(m+4)\\ pgeq P_1^a(r)Bigl(1+fracO(1)pBigr) leq& sum_r3^-r+(log log m)sum_substackrgeq 0\\ P_1^a(r)leq log m3^-r. If P_1^a(r)leq log m, then rgg log fraclog P_1log log m, so that (log log m)sum_substackr\\ P_1^a(r)leq log m3^-rll frac(log log m)^2log P_1ll frac(log log m)^3log mll 1, since P_1geq N^varepsilongg m^varepsilon and varepsilongeq (log log m)^-1.

nodes.statement: We say that a real number widetildebeta is an exceptional zero of level Pgeq 3 and quality kappa in (0,1) if there exists a primitive Dirichlet character widetildechi of some modulus widetilderleq P such that L(widetildebeta,widetildechi)=0 and widetildebeta geq 1-frackappalog P. The character widetildechi is called an exceptional character and widetilder is called the exceptional modulus.

nodes.statement: Let us prove part (2); part (1) is similar but somewhat easier. Similar to the proof of the previous Lemma, we apply Lemma~, but here to multiply by c_E_3^*(n). Every summand is O(1), so for each pair (r,chi) the terms with n<N/R^4 contribute at most Obigl((log N)(N/R^4)/(N/R)bigr)=O(R^-3log N), and O(R^-1log N) in total. Since widetilderleq R and log Rgeq (log N)^4/5, this is Obigl((1-widetildebeta)(log N)exp(-clog N/log R)bigr) by~, once c is small enough. We may therefore restrict to Isubset [N/R^4,N], where~ applies. \label{def:greaterapprox}
    Let $\epsilon>0$ and $f,g$ be finitely supported arithmetic functions. We write $f \gtrapprox_{\epsilon} g$ if there exists a sequence of functions $f_i$, $0\leq i \leq J$ with $f_0=f, f_J=g$ and either $f_i \approx_\epsilon f_{i+1}$ or $f_i\geq f_{i+1}$.

nodes.statement: It is at this point that we use the hierarchy of parameters in Definition~. We now summarise the reasoning and in particular explain why the proof below requires us to work with two roughness scales P_0, P_1, instead of the one scale as in the sketch in the introduction. Proposition~ applies Theorem~ with P=P_0 and R=R_0. Its error term~ is admissible only when both fraclog Nlog P_0 and fraclog P_0log R_0 are large, which requires Nggg P_0ggg R_0. Next, Theorem~ produces in~ a saving of R_0^-1/3, which needs to be sufficient to compensate the loss of D_1 from discarding the sieve weights with Lemma~. This forces D_1ll R_0^1/3.
